cues.t: Listen.
Between the island of Falster, and the islands of Bogø and Møn, there runs a narrow green water.
The old documents call it Gronesund. The green sound.
Kings taxed it. A Swedish army walked across it — on foot, on the ice.
A ruined noblewoman rowed a ferry over it, and told the greatest playwright in Denmark that she had never in her life been happier.
And on one night in 1872, the sea came back over the top of it.
Somewhere along this shore there is a box.
It has been shut since 1711.
You have forty-five minutes.
Summer, 1711.
Plague is loose in Copenhagen, and a young man called Ludvig Holberg is running for his life. South. To the coast. To a ferry house at the edge of the water.
The woman who brings him his supper is called Marie Grubbe.
She was born to one of the great families of Denmark. She was married to the king's own half-brother.
And here she is. In a wet apron. At the end of the world. Telling him she is content.
He wrote about her. He could not stop writing about her.
What he did not write about, was the casket.
She cut one word across five splinters of its lid, and gave them to the sound.
Five stops. Five splinters. Each one carries a letter — and the letter's place in the word.
Gather all five, and whatever is inside is yours.
Off you go.
Five splinters.
The sound gave them up in its own order, not yours. But each one is numbered. Each one knows its place.
One word. Five letters. Danish.
Say it out loud at the water.
Skrin.
It is the Danish for a small chest.
The lid comes up.
And there is no gold in it.
There was never going to be gold in it.
There is a bundle of letters, in a hand that had been taught to write like a nobleman's daughter — because it was one.
There is a paper granting the right to row people across Grønsund, and to keep an inn on the Falster shore.
The last thing she owned. The only thing she wanted.
And there is one line, written the summer the young playwright came and asked her how she could possibly bear it.
Jeg har det bedre nu.
I am better off now.
She died here in 1718.
Holberg never got over it. Neither, frankly, did Denmark.
You may go.
First stop. The water's edge, where the ferry came in.
Stand where you can see across, and think about money.
Everything that ever crossed here — every ox, every barrel, every man on foot — was worth a number to somebody.
The green sound. It is in the written record as early as the 1180s.
And by the 1230s the king's clerks are here with their books — because a crossing is a chokepoint, and a chokepoint is money.
Someone has scratched a note into the margin of the toll board. And the salt has eaten the fourth line.
Read the board. Find the sum.
Thirty-five.
An ox is six, a barrel is four, and a man is one — a man being, as ever, the cheapest thing on the list.
Something comes away from the board in your hand. A splinter of oak, with a letter cut into it.
Second stop. Now look at that water.
And imagine it solid.
Imagine an army walking on it.
The winter the sea turned to stone.
January, 1658. Karl the Tenth Gustav walks his army across the frozen Little Belt. Seven thousand men. On ice. Over open sea.
And he keeps going. Langeland. Lolland. Falster.
Out there, a warship sits frozen into the sound like a fly in amber, and it will not move again until spring.
But the ice is not honest. It is a foot thick here, and rotten twenty paces that way.
The only men who know the difference are the men who fish it. And one of them left directions.
No names. Only steps.
B, four. The mill on the rise.
Of course it is. It is the one thing you can see from out on that ice in any weather.
Second splinter.
Third stop. The ferry house.
This is the one with a body in it.
Now.
Marie Grubbe.
Married at seventeen to Ulrik Frederik Gyldenløve — the king's half-brother, the finest match in the kingdom.
Divorced. Married again. Ruined.
And then, at the bottom of that very long fall, she marries a man twenty years younger than herself, and comes here — to row strangers across a cold strait for coppers.
And when Holberg asks her, with the beautiful rudeness of the young, how she can possibly bear it —
she tells him she is happier now.
The nineteenth of May, 1711. A drinking party at the ferry house goes wrong.
Her husband picks up a gun. And a skipper from Dragør does not go home.
In the hour before the bailiff arrives, a casket leaves that house. Four people watched it go.
And the parish clerk, who knew this village extremely well, wrote in the margin:
exactly one of them is telling the truth.
The loft.
Only the tollman told the truth — and even he only told you what did not happen.
That, right there, is a village. Third splinter.
Fourth stop. Get yourself some height, if this island has any to offer.
You want to be standing where a fire would be seen for miles.
1813. Denmark is at war with Britain.
The whole coast is watched. On every headland there are men sitting up all night beside a heap of tar and brushwood, waiting to set it alight.
One fire lights the next. The country can be told in an hour.
And in the middle of all this, the Postmaster General sits down — and issues a price list.
Because of course he does.
But look at the top of this copy. Somebody else has written on it. In a different hand.
Every fifth word. The fire is lit at Bavnen.
Three place names sitting in plain sight to waste your time, and the real one buried in the grammar.
Fourth splinter.
Last stop. Down to the dike. Or the shore. Somewhere you can see how high the water is today.
Because you are about to find out how high it got.
The thirteenth of November, 1872.
The wind comes round, and it does not stop. Thirty-two metres a second — a hurricane, over Lolland, Falster and Møn.
It pushes the Baltic west. And west. And the water climbs three metres above anything a living person has ever seen.
It comes over the fields in the dark. Close to a hundred people drown on land. Two hundred ships are broken open.
Afterwards, the parish clerk wrote five lines about it.
They are terrible verse. And they are not about the flood.
Diget. The dike.
They read the water, and then they built against it. And it is still standing. And it is the only reason you are standing dry.
That is five.
